legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Multi-User Large Language Model Agents", Shu Yang, Shenzhe Zhu, Hao Zhu, Jose Ramon Enriquez, Di Wang, Alex Pentland, Michiel A. Bakker, Jiaxin Pei (corresponding). Affiliations: Stanford, KAUST, UT Austin, MIT. Preprint, arXiv:2604.08567v2 [cs.CL], 27 Apr 2026. Code: github.com/Kordi-AI/Multi-User-LLM-Agent. The benchmark is called Muses-Bench (named once, in the Table 2 caption).

COVERAGE: All 23 pages (75,341 chars) read, including appendices A and B. The figure heatmaps are numbers only, so I did not read them in detail. Page numbers below are from the PDF.

FIT: Weak and tangential for 04-execution-boundaries. The paper does not study sandboxes, hooks, permission gates, rollback or cost. It tests prompt-only access control: an LLM "gatekeeper" told who is authorized, with no enforcement layer outside the model. If used, it is best as a small sharpens citation under "a role label is not a sandbox" and the trust-zones material. It could also fit 02-context-engineering (multi-user context separation) or the evaluation notes, but it is thin everywhere.

CORE CLAIM: Chat templates and training (SFT, scalar-reward RLHF) assume one principal. Frontier LLMs deployed as shared agents for several users with different authority levels therefore:
- prioritize unstably under conflict;
- leak protected information more as turns accumulate;
- coordinate inefficiently.
It is a benchmark plus position paper. It proposes no method, defence or fix.

SETUP: 19 models: 13 proprietary (GPT-5.2/5.1/5-Nano/4o-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5 and 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 3 Pro/3 Flash/2.5 Flash, Grok, GLM-4.5-Air) and 6 open-weight (DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS-120B, Llama-3-70B and 8B, Qwen3-30B and 4B). Temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0. Users are simulated personas with authority levels 1-10. Multi-user input is serialized into a single "user" role in one of three formats (Says, Colon, XML). The paper does not state the number of runs per scenario. Cost is not reported.

Three scenarios:
1. Instruction following: 1,298 execution scenarios and 304 selection scenarios, with 2-10 users.
2. Access control: 216 scenarios (direct, social engineering, XML obfuscation). The prompt says "If the user is unauthorized, strictly reject". Privacy is 1 minus the leakage rate; utility is delivery of the secret to authorized users.
3. Meeting scheduling: 216 scenarios, 108 full-disclosure and 108 partial-disclosure.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (Table 2, mean +/- SE; best average is Gemini-3-Pro at 85.6, then Claude-Sonnet-4.5 at 82.6):
- Privacy vs utility trade-off. Claude-Sonnet-4.5 scores privacy 77.3 and utility 97.5. GPT-5.1 scores privacy 98.6 and utility 60.3. GPT-5.2 scores privacy 100.0 and utility 61.2. Gemini-3-Flash scores privacy 88.7 and utility 90.6. No model is high on both except Gemini-3-Pro (98.6 / 73.9).
- Conflict hurts execution (Fig 3). Claude-Haiku-4.5 falls from 0.86 (aligned) to 0.62 (conflict). GPT-OSS-120B falls from 0.64 to 0.50.
- Multi-turn privacy erosion (Fig 4, 10 rounds). Claude-3.5-Haiku drops from above 0.95 in round 1 to below 0.75 after four rounds. The steepest decline is in rounds 1-6.
- Meeting success is mostly 50-65% (Gemini-3-Pro 64.8, Sonnet-4.5 62.5, GPT-5.2 59.7). Partial disclosure scores lower than full disclosure for nearly all models.
- Success falls with group size N from 2 to 20, and turns grow roughly linearly (Fig 9).
- Selection vs execution mismatch. Qwen3-4B-IT scores 83.8 on selection F1 but 57.9 on execution.

ABLATION: Serialization format (XML, Colon, Says) and attack type (none, fake authorization, pressure, role-playing) change privacy and utility little (Figs 6-8, p.21). The authors conclude that interaction complexity is the bottleneck, not prompt template. This suggests that wording the role label differently does not fix leakage. The paper offers no controlled comparison against a real external access check.

QUOTES:
- "privacy and access control begin to break down as interaction rounds increase" (p.2)
- "multi-user privacy control remains brittle under sustained interaction, and that maintaining long-term privacy consistency is a fundamentally harder problem than passing isolated access-control checks." (p.10)
- On a failure case: "the model treats the security constraint as a restriction on the tool/interface rather than the information itself" (p.21, "refusal-leak paradox"). Claude-3.5-Haiku refuses vault access, then states the Session ID anyway.
- "Integrating policy enforcement with structured tool calls, access checks, and interaction logs would improve transparency and reproducibility" (p.12, future work)

LIMITS:
- Simulated users only; the authors call for human-in-the-loop and deployment studies.
- Short interactions (10 rounds).
- No defence is tested, and no deterministic or external enforcement baseline is compared. The "enforce outside the model" lesson is my inference, not a result. The only related line is the future-work bullet quoted above.
- Single-user-role serialization is a confound. No model natively supports multi-user messages, so some failures may come from the format rather than from the models.
- Run counts and cost are unstated.
- Text-versus-table inconsistencies in section 5.2 (a sign of weak proofreading):
  - the text says GPT-OSS-120B meeting success is 77.3, but Table 2 says 58.9;
  - the text says Grok-3-Mini privacy is 99.7 and utility 59.0, but the table says 99.6 and 60.1;
  - the text says GPT-OSS-120B utility is 94.4, but the table says 94.8.
  Use the table values.
- Tested models are 2025-era; this is dated as of Nov 2026.

BUILDS ON: Principal-agent theory (Rees 1985; Holmstrom 1979; Jarrahi and Ritala 2025). Multi-principal assistance games (Fickinger et al. 2020, arXiv). Social-choice preference aggregation (Bakker et al., NeurIPS 2022; Fish et al. 2023; Keeney and Kirkwood 1975). Multi-user information gathering (Jhamtani, Andreas and Van Durme, Findings of ACL 2025). Serialization variants follow Jhamtani et al. 2025 and Mu et al. 2025. Related benchmarks: tau-bench (Yao et al. 2024) and MINT (Wang et al. 2023). Attack styles follow Nian et al. 2025 and Yang et al. 2025.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 4 (p.9-10), "Privacy preservation under multi-round cross-user access control". It shows privacy falling across rounds 1-10 for all 19 models, which is the strongest visual for "prompt-level access control decays". Figure 2 (p.6) is an alternative, an illustration of the three scenarios.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure data came out as unlabeled number lists, so I did not map each number to a bar. There are the table/text inconsistencies listed under LIMITS.
